unit.title: How iOS chooses work and protects shared state
unit.summary: See why a timer can wait, how queues choose work, how locks protect a change, and how tasks share worker threads.

lessons.title: RunLoop: choosing events, timers and display updates
lessons.summary: Explain why a ready timer can wait during a scroll, how display callbacks differ, and when each registration must stop.
objectives: Predict whether a timer can run in the current mode, including a mode registered as common.
Tell a timer, an event source, an observer and a display link apart.
Name what keeps each callback alive and when to invalidate its registration.
Explain what a host test proves and what needs an iOS screen or device trace.

sections.title: A due event may still have to wait
sections.html:
A reminder can be due while you are looking at a different list. An iOS RunLoop works with a similar choice: a mode is the collection of registered events it is currently checking. The loop handles those events on its thread, usually the main thread for UI work. An Android Handler also sends callbacks to a thread's Looper. In both systems, a slow callback keeps that thread busy. The extra iOS rule is mode membership: a ready callback in another mode can remain waiting. A default-mode timer can therefore pause during scrolling without being cancelled.

The system supplies a run loop associated with each thread as needed. The application frameworks drive the main loop. Creating a background DispatchQueue does not create a permanently running RunLoop for its blocks, nor does retrieving RunLoop.current start an event-processing loop. Worker-thread designs that require an event loop must deliberately install sources, manage lifetime and drive it; most application features should prefer established asynchronous APIs instead. A queue and a run loop solve different coordination problems.

Session 038 already explains frame deadlines and main-thread costs. Here the new question is eligibility: which work may run during which event-processing phase? Separate three hypotheses before debugging a late callback: the timer was invalidated, the active mode excludes it, or the thread was occupied by another callback. Changing an interval does not distinguish those cases. Capture registration mode, ownership, and observed callback order before making a scheduling change.

sections.title: Choose which modes may handle the timer
sections.html:
A mode names a collection of work the loop may handle. RunLoop.Mode.default is the ordinary event-processing mode; UIKit also uses tracking behavior during interactions. The loop runs one selected mode at a time. The name .common is a registration shortcut for the modes designated common on that loop. Adding a timer there includes it in that selected set. It does not add the timer to every custom mode, give it higher priority, or let it interrupt a busy callback. First ask which activities should include this timer, then choose its registrations.

Choose the timer's modes from what the feature needs. A progress indicator may need to keep updating while the user scrolls. Nonessential polling may be allowed to wait. Registering every timer in common modes adds work during interaction, exactly when the main thread needs time to respond. Record the reason for each timer's choice. A custom mode belongs in a controlled scratch experiment; it is not a way to bypass UIKit's event loop in production.

The host companion installs an already due one-shot timer in RuntimeLab.synthetic. It pumps default mode for a bounded interval and checks that no callback occurred, then pumps the custom mode and checks exactly one callback. This establishes mode eligibility for that host fixture. It does not reproduce UIKit tracking or a physical display. CFRunLoopRunInMode is a Core Foundation function that bounds this artificial probe; its final Boolean requests return after a source is handled. Timers have special treatment and need not cause that early return. Never pump nested application loops to make synchronous code wait for an async result: unrelated events can reenter your supposedly atomic flow.

sections.title: Count time from a deadline, not from ticks
sections.html:
A timer asks for a callback when a time arrives. It cannot make a busy thread respond immediately. Foundation's scheduledTimer convenience installs the timer on the current loop in default mode; creating a Timer directly leaves installation to you. A repeating timer follows its planned cadence. After missing several firings, it does not replay an unlimited stack of ticks. For a ten-second countdown, a callback at second four should show six seconds left even if only one callback ran. Compute that result from a deadline. Calendar dates can jump when the clock changes; elapsed time needs a clock that moves forward.

Tolerance is extra delay you allow after the planned firing time. The system can use it to combine wakeups and save energy. It does not authorize early firing or create a real-time guarantee. A callback delayed by a busy thread or excluded mode can be later still. Choose a tolerance from the feature's acceptable staleness and energy goals. A UI refresh every millisecond is not justified merely because the API accepts a small number.

The run loop keeps a scheduled timer alive. A block timer can also keep captured objects alive; a target timer retains its target. If the owner retains the timer too, those strong references can form a cycle. Define a stop method and call invalidate on the installation thread when the feature ends. Weak capture removes one strong edge, but does not remove the repeating registration. A request launched by an earlier tick may still finish after teardown. Request its cancellation and check freshness before publishing. Catch errors inside the timer callback, because errors cannot be thrown across that framework callback boundary. Then apply the stated stop or retry policy.

sections.title: An event source brings work; an observer watches the loop
sections.html:
An event source tells the loop there is work to handle. Core Foundation calls manually signalled sources source zero and port-based sources source one. For a custom source, your code signals readiness and may also need to wake the sleeping loop. A port-based source gets help from the system kernel, which manages low-level events. These names describe event delivery, not kinds of Swift Task. Foundation often hides them behind an easier API. Timers have their own special handling, so a timer firing does not necessarily make a run-loop call return as an input source would.

A CFRunLoopObserver receives selected activity notifications such as entry, before timers, before sources, before waiting, after waiting and exit. It lets an instrumented scratch target observe event-loop transitions. It is not an executor, a replacement for synchronization, or proof that every frame rendered. Its callback occurs on the observed loop's thread; logging large payloads or doing network work there perturbs the loop you are trying to understand. Keep recorded events bounded and distinguish observation overhead from application cost.

Ownership applies to observers and sources as well. Remove or invalidate registrations when their owning experiment or feature ends. Inspect callback captures, and do not use one registration token to imply several unrelated resources were cleaned up. Foundation RunLoop is generally not thread-safe; call its methods in the context of its thread. Core Foundation provides selected cross-thread operations, but that does not make arbitrary Foundation calls safe. A source signaling design should specify which documented operation wakes the loop and which thread performs registration and removal. The companion's same-thread, bounded probe avoids that additional contract.

sections.title: Ask the display when to update
sections.html:
A moving dot should update with the display, rather than guess that a frame always lasts sixteen milliseconds. CADisplayLink calls you in step with display updates. Android Choreographer is a useful comparison. Its timestamp and targetTimestamp describe the relevant frame interval when subtracted. The device, power policy and temperature can change that interval. Sixty and one hundred twenty hertz are possible rates, not universal promises. Preferred frame-rate settings express a request. Other rendering work still needs time, so the whole interval is not available for your callback.

import UIKit
@MainActor
final class DisplayDriver: NSObject {
    private var link: CADisplayLink?
    func start() {
        stop()
        let next = CADisplayLink(target: self, selector: #selector(tick(_:)))
        next.add(to: .main, forMode: .common)
        link = next
    }
    @objc private func tick(_ link: CADisplayLink) {
        let frameInterval = link.targetTimestamp - link.timestamp
        print(frameInterval) // Teaching only; omit per-frame console I/O in a real animation.
    }
    func stop() { link?.invalidate(); link = nil }
}

This snippet requires an iOS UIKit target; the companion Targets/DisplayDriver.swift has the same lifecycle pattern without per-frame console output. import supplies UIKit and its display-link exposure. NSObject supports Objective-C selector dispatch. @MainActor constrains calls and state. The optional property means no link is owned initially. start first stops an older registration, constructs a link whose target is self, registers it on the main loop's common modes, then retains it. @objc exposes tick to the selector runtime; the underscore removes the external argument label. stop invalidates before clearing the reference. The owning controller must call stop: deinit alone cannot break a cycle that prevents deinitialization.

sections.title: Read the scheduler choice before diagnosing a delay
sections.html:
Debounce waits for a quiet interval before forwarding a value. The referral-info binding combines validation values, removes repeats, and uses debounce with RunLoop.main. That line names the scheduler chosen for the delay. It does not tell us which timer modes Combine uses internally or show that scrolling caused a fault. Follow the publisher's lifetime and the object retaining its subscription before changing the scheduler. Cancelling a subscription ends that API's work according to its contract; invalidating a Timer ends a timer registration. Related cleanup goals do not make those APIs interchangeable.

A useful debugging worksheet lists event, expected owner, registration mode, time basis, eligible callback and cleanup event. Compare a default-mode timer, common-mode timer and display link in an independent UIKit screen containing a scroll view. Record callback counts and timestamps during idle, dragging and deceleration. Counts alone cannot identify the reason for a gap; correlate activity and thread work in a trace. Do not manufacture a slow callback in the company client.

On Android, removing Handler callbacks or Choreographer frame callbacks also matters for screen ownership. However, Android's message queue does not expose the same run-loop common-mode registration contract. Learn the iOS mechanism rather than renaming a Looper. The host probe verifies only a synthetic custom-mode contrast. UIKit tracking, observers in a live screen, variable refresh rate and energy implications remain target or device investigations, with no results claimed by this lesson.

quiz.question: A default-only timer stops visibly updating while the UI tracks a gesture. Which explanation should you investigate?
options: Tracking can use a mode that does not monitor that timer.
The timer automatically cancels on every touch.
Common mode gives callbacks a hard real-time deadline.
quiz.explanation: Mode membership determines eligibility. Invalidation and main-thread occupancy are separate hypotheses; common registration neither cancels nor guarantees a deadline.

quiz.question: Which countdown policy tolerates delayed or skipped timer firings?
options: Subtract exactly one second on every callback.
Recompute remaining time from the chosen deadline and clock.
Launch a new repeating timer after every callback.
quiz.explanation: A timer offers callback opportunities and can skip missed firings. The chosen clock defines the time contract; callback count is not elapsed time.

quiz.question: Why must the display driver's owner call stop explicitly?
options: The selector compiler cannot access private methods.
The run loop and display link can retain a target, so deinit may never begin.
Setting preferredFramesPerSecond to zero invalidates a link.
quiz.explanation: Invalidation removes the registration and target association. Clearing a property or relying on deinit does not reliably dismantle the owning cycle.

exercise.brief: Predict the host timer's two callback counts. Then plan a separate iOS screen that compares ordinary timers, common-mode timers and display updates.
steps: Read checkRunLoopMode. Write the expected count after each phase before running it.
Use the isolated command in the RuntimeLab README and save your actual host result.
In a separate iOS scratch target, place default-mode and common-mode timers plus the supplied display driver beside a scroll view.
Choose when the screen stops this work. List which objects keep each timer, link and callback alive.
Describe the observations that would separate a timer excluded by its mode from a thread occupied by a slow callback.
acceptance: The host default-mode phase records 0 custom-timer callbacks; the custom-mode phase records 1.
The iOS plan names its target requirements and gives each callback only a small amount of work.
Each timer and display link is invalidated on its installation thread at a named stop event.
The report labels completed host checks and any iOS or device steps still to be run.
exercise.solution:
The timer's due time has arrived, but the loop must also check the right mode. Default mode excludes the timer registered in RuntimeLab.synthetic, so the count stays 0. Running the named custom mode handles the timer once and makes the count 1. This one-shot timer invalidates itself after delivery. The defer also provides cleanup if an earlier assertion throws. The Core Foundation calls each have a time limit, so a failed prediction becomes a reported host error rather than an intentionally hung process.

Use one UIKit controller to own two timers and one DisplayDriver. Start them on MainActor when the screen enters the chosen active state. Invalidate both timers and call driver.stop when that state ends. Store only small synthetic counts and timestamp samples. Capture the controller weakly in a timer block, but still explicitly remove the registration. Build the separate scratch target before trying gestures. During a drag, compare both timer traces with the interaction. This comparison cannot promise a display cadence or reveal Combine's internal scheduling.

If every callback disappears while a synchronous decode occupies the main thread, adding a common-mode registration cannot free that thread. Give the expensive work a separate execution and ownership design. If only the default timer pauses while common-mode callbacks continue, the observations support a mode explanation. Keep the platform and observed order with your report. These are acceptance rules for interpreting your experiment, not claims that a UIKit run or learner exercise already succeeded.

simple.story: A caretaker has two trays of reminder cards: ordinary work and a special inspection. A bell says an inspection reminder is due. The caretaker is looking only at the ordinary tray, so that reminder stays waiting. Later, the caretaker opens the inspection tray and handles it. The bell did not cancel the card. Its time had arrived, but its tray was not being checked. A reminder placed in several agreed trays can be seen during more activities. It still has to wait if the caretaker is busy handling another card.
simple.meaning: A RunLoop checks events on a thread. Its current mode chooses which registered events it can handle. A due timer registered only in another mode can stay waiting. Registering in common modes includes it in a selected group of modes.

example.before: A one-shot timer in RuntimeLab.synthetic is already due. Its callback count is 0.
example.change: Run the loop in default mode, then run it in RuntimeLab.synthetic, using the bounded host probe.
example.after: The default phase leaves the count at 0. The custom-mode phase makes it 1 because that mode includes the timer.

picture.caption: The host timer becomes due before the loop checks its registered mode.

items.label: Timer due
items.text: The synthetic timer is ready; its count is 0.

items.label: Default mode
items.text: This mode excludes the synthetic timer, so the count stays 0.

items.label: Synthetic mode
items.text: This mode includes the timer, so the callback makes the count 1.

words.meaning: A thread's event loop, which checks registered work and waits when it has nothing to handle.
A named collection of events the loop can check during one run.
A selected set of modes that share registrations; it does not include every possible mode.
An allowed delay that can help combine timer wakeups; it does not promise the callback will be punctual.
Ending a timer or display-link registration so it no longer asks for callbacks.
A callback source coordinated with display updates, rather than a guessed fixed timer interval.

simple.remember: Being due and being eligible in the current mode are separate conditions.
simple.boundary: A mode is a registration rule, not a physical tray or a worker. The host custom-mode result does not reproduce UIKit scrolling, reveal Combine's timer modes, or guarantee a display deadline.

lessons.title: Queues and operations: choosing order, waits and stop requests
lessons.summary: Choose how queued work may overlap, spot a cycle of waits, and keep an operation's readiness separate from its result.
objectives: Explain separately how a queue runs work and whether the caller waits after submitting it.
Use quality of service as an importance hint without promising a deadline or order across queues.
Track the owners and cleanup of groups, barriers, event sources and work items.
Draw operation dependencies and choose how to handle success, failure and limited capacity.

sections.title: A queue chooses order and overlap
sections.html:
A queue is a place to submit work with rules about when it may run. On a serial DispatchQueue, one item runs at a time. On a concurrent queue, items may overlap. Android's ExecutorService gives you a familiar starting point, but a serial dispatch queue usually does not own a permanent thread. Apart from the main queue, the system chooses execution threads. A rule about order therefore does not establish which thread will call you. If an API needs one specific thread, or a lock must be released by its acquiring thread, state that requirement separately.

sync waits for its work to finish before returning. async submits work and returns without waiting for completion. These describe the caller's waiting behavior, independently of whether the destination is serial or concurrent. A serial async queue can be the right design for serialized state changes. A concurrent sync call still blocks the caller until its item finishes; it does not grant the caller extra UI responsiveness.

Quality of service expresses the importance and latency character of work, with categories such as userInteractive, userInitiated, utility and background. Assign it from user need rather than escalating every operation. QoS is neither a deadline nor a FIFO rule across competing queues. A serial queue provides ordering for its own submitted items; independent producers still have a race over submission order. On a concurrent queue, do not infer completion order. This lesson extends session 015's task-lifetime model to legacy queue work: dispatch blocks have no automatically owned Swift task tree.

sections.title: Draw who waits for whom
sections.html:
Imagine a clerk refusing to finish a card until the next card is handled. If the same clerk must handle that next card, neither can finish. A deadlock is this cycle of waits. Calling sync on the serial queue already running your callback creates that cycle: the new item waits for the callback to return, while the callback waits for the item. Dispatch can detect some misuse, but detection is not a safety plan. The main queue has the same risk. A main thread waiting for a worker that waits for the main queue creates an indirect cycle too.

Review every blocking edge and every callback destination. A worker's sync to a separate serial queue can be valid in a synchronous host program, provided the destination cannot depend on that worker. A Swift cooperative task should generally suspend for async work rather than block on a DispatchGroup or semaphore. The companion's bounded waits run only in synchronous host probes; none waits for the main queue. It never demonstrates deadlock by deliberately hanging.

A queue-specific value or dispatchPrecondition can enforce an API's expected calling context. Neither repairs a cycle automatically. An abstraction should choose whether methods must be called off its queue, are asynchronous throughout, or expose a narrowly reviewed reentrant fast path. Recursive direct execution can violate ordering and invariants if added casually. A public callback invoked while inside queue-owned state can reenter the same cache; dispatching that callback later or copying a result before leaving the protected context often creates a clearer contract. Errors inside async blocks need explicit Result or completion handling because throwing cannot cross an escaping block that returns Void.

sections.title: A group tracks completion, not success
sections.html:
A DispatchGroup is a count of work still outstanding. async(group:) adds and removes its block automatically. When you manage the count yourself, every enter needs exactly one leave, including on failure and cancellation. notify schedules a callback after the count reaches zero. wait keeps the caller's thread occupied until completion or timeout. A timeout means the wait ended; it does not stop the unfinished work. For three jobs, a count reaching zero tells you all three finished. You still need stored results to know whether any failed.

let queue = DispatchQueue(label: "example.serial", qos: .utility)
let group = DispatchGroup()
let values = LockedValue<[Int]>([])
for index in 0..<3 {
    queue.async(group: group) { values.update { $0.append(index) } }
}
guard group.wait(timeout: .now() + 5) == .success else {
    throw LabError.failed("unfinished batch")
}
let output = values.snapshot()

This host fragment runs inside a throwing function with Foundation/Dispatch imports and the companion's LockedValue and LabError declarations. queue is serial, group tracks its submitted blocks, and values protects observations independently. The half-open range includes zero through two. Each closure captures its iteration's immutable index. update passes protected storage inout to a synchronous closure. The guard rejects a failed bounded wait, and snapshot occurs only after completion. The expected output is [0, 1, 2]. An otherwise similar concurrent queue would require membership checks instead of assuming array order.

A group supplies no error storage or sibling cancellation. Collect Result values under a lock or serial owner and decide all-or-nothing versus partial completion separately. Java CompletableFuture.allOf has a familiar join role but has its own exceptional-completion behavior; do not import those semantics into DispatchGroup. UIKit code should prefer notification or an asynchronous bridge instead of copying this CLI wait.

sections.title: Keep every protected access on the same queue
sections.html:
A barrier is an exclusive turn on your own concurrent queue. Earlier items on that queue finish first, the barrier runs without other items from that queue, then later items may begin. This can protect a cache only if every read and write uses that same boundary. A direct field read or work on another queue can bypass it. A global concurrent queue does not provide this private barrier protection. On a serial queue, items already run one at a time; a barrier flag does not create concurrent readers or a wider lock.

The inspected Cache constructs a serial queue without the concurrent attribute, uses sync getters, and submits setters with barrier flags. That is evidence of asynchronous mutation and serialized queue ownership, not an example of concurrent readers protected by barriers. Its findOrCreate executes a caller fallback inside queue.sync: review callback reentry and expensive fallback work as potential risks, without claiming an observed failure. Understand actual queue creation before assigning meaning to a flag.

A DispatchSource asks for callbacks when an event occurs, such as a timer firing or a file descriptor becoming readable. A descriptor is the system's handle for an open resource. Several events can be combined into one callback; this is called coalescing. The companion's user-data-add source checks the aggregate value, activates a newly created source once, then cancels and observes its cancellation handler. A descriptor source needs a documented descriptor owner and close policy, commonly closing in the cancellation handler after event handling has ended. Cancelling is asynchronous cleanup, not permission to free resources immediately. Source handlers can retain a source or owner; dismantle those edges after cancellation. Dispatch timers likewise do not supply exact deadlines; choose leeway and callback costs deliberately.

sections.title: A stop request needs a cooperating owner
sections.html:
Cancellation is a request, not a hand reaching in to stop instructions. DispatchWorkItem wraps work and records whether cancellation was requested. Cancelling before its body starts can prevent that body from running. After it starts, long work needs to check a stop flag or the work item's cancellation state and leave safely. Cleanup still has to happen. For a delayed search update, also check that its request identity is still current before publishing; an old request can race with a newer one. Keep the work-item handle where the owner can request cancellation later.

The companion cancels a work item before submitting it, drains the serial queue from the external host caller, and checks that its side effect is absent. That deterministic schedule proves only pre-execution cancellation for that fixture. It does not establish in-flight stopping or deadline behavior. A cancellable closure capturing its own work item can create a retain cycle if carelessly stored; a small locked cancellation token or explicit owner often gives a simpler graph.

Operation.cancel and DispatchWorkItem.cancel set their own stop state. They do not automatically cancel an enclosing Swift Task, and cancelling that task does not automatically cancel them. An adapter must connect these requests explicitly when the underlying API supports stopping. Keep ordinary errors and cancellation recognisable; an empty default result can hide both. Java Future.cancel has interruption options with different guarantees, and Thread.interrupt is also cooperative. Kotlin Job cancellation follows its coroutine hierarchy. A dispatch block does not acquire such a hierarchy just because an async function launched it.

sections.title: Check readiness first, then inspect the result
sections.html:
An operation becomes ready when its prerequisites have finished and its other readiness rules allow it to start. OperationQueue chooses among ready Operation objects using priorities and dependencies. maxConcurrentOperationCount limits how many operations execute, not how many waiting objects or large captures remain queued. Add dependencies before enqueueing, and draw an acyclic graph, with no path leading back to itself. Dependencies may cross queues. Even a queue limited to one executing operation needs explicit dependencies when one result must precede another; the limit alone does not express that requirement.

In the host fixture, the consumer is submitted before the producer but depends on it. The producer stores a synthetic failure Result; the consumer observes that failure and records recovery. Dependence means the producer reached finished, not that it succeeded. Cancelling a producer also does not automatically make dependent business work fail or disappear. A cancelled operation may be finished without useful output, so design absent-output and failure branches explicitly. Dependencies wait for isFinished, not an arbitrary completion callback's downstream UI action.

BlockOperation is useful for finite synchronous bodies. Starting a callback-based network request inside it and returning immediately marks the operation complete before that request ends. A genuine asynchronous Operation subclass must correctly maintain isExecuting, isFinished, readiness and KVO transitions, including cancellation before start and exactly one terminal transition. That specialist implementation is not supplied here. Queues retain unfinished operations, and closures retain captures; permanently suspended queues and dependency cycles can retain work forever. Select OperationQueue for a real readiness graph or legacy integration, not to imitate structured task cancellation. The worked exercise makes dependency order, error interpretation and cleanup observable without requiring any client modification.

The full runnable companion selects Swift 6.2 tools and macOS 15 because it also includes modern executor and Mutex examples. Dispatch and OperationQueue are older APIs; that package floor is not their introduction date. Its Foundation/Dispatch host checks ran on the recorded Apple toolchain only, and establish neither Linux support nor an iOS app build.

quiz.question: What changes when you use async with a serial queue?
options: The queue becomes concurrent.
The caller returns before completion while the queue still serializes items.
The block receives its own permanent thread.
quiz.explanation: Caller waiting and destination concurrency are independent. Thread selection is a separate implementation concern.

quiz.question: A producer operation finishes with a failure Result. What does its dependency guarantee to a consumer?
options: The producer succeeded.
The consumer is automatically cancelled.
The readiness prerequisite finished; the consumer still needs an error policy.
quiz.explanation: Dependency readiness uses finished state, which includes cancellation and failure. Business success must be represented and inspected separately.

quiz.question: Which barrier design protects concurrent cache accesses?
options: Barrier writes on a global queue and direct reads anywhere.
All reads and barrier writes through one owned custom concurrent queue.
Barrier flags on any queue provide an application-wide mutex.
quiz.explanation: Barrier exclusivity has a queue scope. Bypassing that queue or using global-queue barriers defeats the stated ownership design.

exercise.brief: In your scratch copy, give the producer three possible outcomes: value, error, or cancellation before it starts. Make the consumer handle each using a dependency.
steps: Run the finite host probes using the README command and keep the results.
Explain why the consumer waits even though it is submitted first.
In your own scratch copy, let the producer call a closure that returns a Result.
Add a producer cancelled before start. Give the consumer a branch for missing output.
Draw the main-to-worker-to-main wait cycle on paper and explain how an asynchronous reply removes it.
acceptance: Success uses its value; failure follows a named recovery policy.
The producer cancelled before start does not run its body, and the consumer handles the missing result.
addDependency sets the required order; enqueue order and QoS are not used as substitutes.
Each manual completion signal is balanced. Waits have time limits and run outside UI and cooperative task executors.
exercise.solution:
Store the producer's optional Result behind one lock, and keep a separate event log. For success, store .success(17). For failure, store .failure(.fixture). Cancellation before the body starts leaves nil. Give the consumer three branches: apply 17, record the chosen recovery for the error, or record that its prerequisite stopped without output. Capture an immutable scenario value in the producer so later enqueues cannot change which case it represents.

Add consumer.addDependency(producer) before enqueueing either operation. The consumer must then wait until the producer reaches finished. Submitting the consumer first makes the fixture check this rule instead of accidentally relying on arrival order. Have the consumer signal completion to the host, with a finite wait, and inspect the event log afterward. That signal reports completion; the stored Result carries the output. If you also cancel the consumer, do not expect its body to record a recovery event. Check its finished state and lack of side effects instead.

The shipped baseline checks failure recovery and a separate BlockOperation cancelled before start. Build the three-outcome fixture yourself. For a dispatch source, wait for its cancellation handler before reclaiming a descriptor. For a group timeout, report unfinished work rather than assuming it was stopped. Keep QoS as an importance hint. The main-thread-to-worker-to-main drawing has a wait cycle. An asynchronous reply removes the blocking dependency; you can explain that repair without hanging a process.

simple.story: Two cooks prepare dinner. Mira makes soup. Arun can serve it only after Mira finishes. Arun writes a serving card first, then attaches a note saying it depends on the soup card. The cards' arrival order does not change that rule. If Mira finishes by reporting a broken stove, Arun's turn can still begin, but there is no soup to serve. Arun must read the result and choose another meal. A note saying stop asks a cook to stop safely; it cannot pull a spoon out of a moving hand.
simple.meaning: OperationQueue uses dependencies to decide when an operation is ready. A finished prerequisite may have succeeded, failed, or produced no result. The dependent operation must check that result. Cancellation requests stopping; running work must cooperate and clean up.

example.before: A producer has no stored Result. A consumer depends on that producer and is submitted first.
example.change: Let the producer finish by storing .failure(.fixture).
example.after: The consumer becomes ready after the producer finishes. It sees failure and records recovery instead of applying a value. Submission order did not override the dependency.

picture.caption: The host failure fixture orders two operations and handles the producer's result.

items.label: Dependency
items.text: The consumer is submitted first but must wait for the producer.

items.label: Producer finishes
items.text: The producer stores .failure(.fixture), then reaches finished.

items.label: Consumer checks
items.text: The consumer reads the failure and records recovery.

words.meaning: A queue that runs one submitted work item at a time; it usually has no dedicated thread.
Submission that waits for the submitted work to finish before returning to the caller.
Submission that returns without waiting for the submitted work to finish.
A hint about how urgent work is, rather than a deadline or a guarantee of order.
A prerequisite that must reach finished before an operation becomes ready.
A request to stop; it does not forcibly interrupt instructions already running.

simple.remember: Ready to run does not mean the prerequisite succeeded.
simple.boundary: OperationQueue schedules code, not cooks, and does not know what a business result means. A dependency waits for finished, not successful output or a later UI callback. Dispatch blocks also have no automatic Swift task tree.

lessons.title: Locks: protect one whole change to shared state
lessons.summary: Use a short lock scope to protect a complete change, release it on errors, and call other code after unlocking.
objectives: List every read and write that must belong to one protected change.
Use a scoped lock that releases on errors and never stays held across await.
Choose Mutex or an allocated unfair lock after checking compiler and platform support.
Set one order for taking multiple locks and resume callbacks after releasing them.

sections.title: Protect the read and the write together
sections.html:
Two callbacks can both read a counter at 1 and both write 2. One update disappears even though each callback added one. A protected change must cover reading, deciding and writing together. An invariant is the rule the change preserves, such as one increment for each accepted callback. In Swift, simultaneous unsynchronised accesses that include a write can also be a data race, which is a language safety failure beyond the lost-update example. A lock beside the property is not enough. Every read and write must actually use the same protection.

Synchronous locks are appropriate for short state transitions used from synchronous callbacks: a registration table, terminal-state flag, or snapshot cache. An actor instead sets rules for access to its state; that is isolation, not a dedicated thread. A caller can suspend while awaiting access, freeing its current thread. Another actor job can run when an async method suspends, so isolation does not reserve the whole method across await. Session 016 explains this interleaving, called reentrancy. Here the added skill is choosing a synchronous critical section and auditing every exit, callback and state escape.

Protect the whole compound operation. Locking a getter and setter separately permits two callers to read the same old value and lose one update. Likewise, synchronizing an array mutation but returning its mutable reference elements can leave reachable state unprotected. Define the unit of protection on paper: count plus generation, or current result plus waiter list. A useful API returns a value snapshot or takes a synchronous closure operating on private storage. Kotlin's kotlinx.coroutines Mutex is a suspending lock, whereas NSLock blocks a thread; the names alone conceal that important resource distinction.

sections.title: Keep the lock and its state behind a small API
sections.html:
A lock lets one caller access protected state while other callers wait. NSLock is a Foundation lock with a rule: do not acquire it again while you already hold it. The wrapper below keeps both the lock and its value private. update is a short synchronous visit to that value, and defer releases the lock even if the visit throws. The companion uses Foundation in a macOS host package. The whole package requires Swift 6.2 because another helper uses @concurrent; that tools requirement is not NSLock's introduction date.

final class LockedValue<Value: Sendable>: @unchecked Sendable {
    private let lock = NSLock()
    private var value: Value
    init(_ value: Value) { self.value = value }
    func update<Result>(_ body: (inout Value) throws -> Result) rethrows -> Result {
        lock.lock()
        defer { lock.unlock() }
        return try body(&value)
    }
    func snapshot() -> Value { update { $0 } }
}

final forbids subclass overrides from adding unsynchronized fields. Value is a generic parameter constrained to Sendable; that constraint does not automatically synchronize its containing variable. The lock and value are private to prevent direct bypass. init's underscore permits LockedValue(0). update accepts a synchronous throwing closure with inout access to storage; Result is its independently inferred return type. rethrows means update throws only when that closure throws. lock acquires exclusivity, defer releases it on normal return or error, and try propagates the closure's error. snapshot uses the same path and returns a value.

@unchecked Sendable is an author promise that the compiler does not prove. Its justification is the private state and complete lock coverage; adding a new field requires renewed review. This teaching wrapper is intentionally small and exposes arbitrary closure execution only inside the synthetic lab. Production public APIs should narrow callbacks or document nonreentrancy, because a body that calls snapshot on the same instance deadlocks. Sendable reference values can themselves own mutable state; returning them does not extend this wrapper's lock to that state.

sections.title: Mutex keeps the protected value with the lock
sections.html:
A locked box is easier to audit than a key stored far from its notebook. Swift's Synchronization.Mutex contains both a nonrecursive lock and its protected state. Nonrecursive means the current holder must not acquire it again. Apple lists availability from iOS and iPadOS 18, macOS 15, tvOS 18, watchOS 11 and visionOS 2. Your compiler must also supply the Synchronization module. Installing new tools does not put a new runtime API on an old phone. For an older deployment target, choose a supported fallback or guard availability before using this design.

A simple host declaration is let count = Mutex(0). count.withLock { $0 += 1 } mutates the contained integer synchronously, and count.withLock { $0 } reads its snapshot. let makes the lock binding stable while its protected state still changes. The closure parameter represents exclusive access during the call; do not store access to that state elsewhere. Mutex is noncopyable and carries a compiler-enforced ownership model, so teaching it as a freely copied NSLock object would miss its contract.

Mutex blocks a contending thread. Kotlin's coroutine Mutex instead suspends waiters, so the shared name hides a resource difference. withLock accepts synchronous work and cannot await. An async method can call a short synchronous helper that uses it, then await after the helper returns. Keeping state and lock together makes review easier; it does not prevent deadlock or starvation. Unknown callbacks, inconsistent lock order and large parsing jobs still create risks. Where valid, compute a candidate outside the lock, then validate and apply a small change inside. Validate again because protected state may have changed during the computation.

sections.title: Use a lock with a stable place in memory
sections.html:
A low-level C lock needs its storage to stay at a stable address. OSAllocatedUnfairLock supplies that allocated storage and a scoped withLock API. Its initialState initializer keeps the protected state with it. Unfair means waiting callers have no guaranteed first-in-first-out order; it does not mean the lock is broken. Apple supports this wrapper from iOS and iPadOS 16, macOS 13, tvOS 16 and watchOS 9; check annotations for other targets. The companion imports os and increments an OSAllocatedUnfairLock(initialState: 0). No raw lock pointer is needed for that example.

A raw os_unfair_lock stored as a Swift value is hazardous because Swift values do not give the stable address assumed by the low-level C API. Passing an ampersand does not turn temporary exclusive access into a permanent storage guarantee. Apple's allocated wrapper avoids that pitfall. Although represented as a struct, copied wrapper instances control the same underlying lock allocation, rather than independent locks with copied state. That differs from Mutex's noncopyable ownership and from ordinary value-type copy expectations.

Unfair describes the absence of a fairness guarantee; do not promise waiting callers FIFO service or deadlines. The wrapper is nonrecursive: attempting reacquisition on the owning thread is erroneous. Manual unlock must occur on the same thread that locked it. A task can suspend and resume on another thread, so do not hold this lock or NSLock across await. Even if a particular run stays on one thread, blocking an executor while holding a lock can prevent progress. Prefer withLock for a synchronous transition, then await outside and validate on return. Cancellation does not release a manually acquired lock; structured scope and defer supply synchronous cleanup.

sections.title: Take locks in one order, then call outside them
sections.html:
If one caller holds key A while waiting for B, and another holds B while waiting for A, both can wait forever. Prevent that cycle by choosing one acquisition order. For two protected accounts, ascending immutable account ID can supply the order. Every path needing both locks must follow it. A successful test does not establish that all paths comply; reviewing the paths does. Releasing one lock before taking the other avoids nesting, but can expose half of a transfer. Use that alternative only if the business rule allows the intermediate state or validates and retries it.

Do not execute network I/O, a large decode, notification delivery, delegate callbacks or continuation resumption while holding the lock unless their complete synchronous behavior is explicitly justified. The common pattern is to copy pending callbacks and mark terminal state while locked, release, then notify. This prevents callbacks from reentering an incompletely updated state and keeps lock occupancy small. If the callback needs new information afterward, provide an immutable snapshot or generation token rather than mutable borrowed storage.

Errors need exactly the same coverage as success. defer in the NSLock wrapper releases on thrown closure errors. A failure branch should not skip terminal state cleanup or leave waiters parked forever. Cancellation handlers can race normal callbacks, so the lock may protect a terminal enum that decides exactly one winner and transfers out the continuation. Resume outside the critical section. This unit does not reimplement the full cancellation-aware continuation adapter from other concurrency lessons; it establishes the synchronous state-transition rule that makes such an adapter reviewable. Never use cancellation as a substitute for finishing the locked transition.

sections.title: Check the boundary before declaring it safe
sections.html:
A continuation represents a paused task that another operation will resume. The inspected SubprocessHandle in OvernightKit uses separate NSLocks for buffer, exit and EOF state. EOF means end of input. recordExit stores the exit code and removes its waiting continuations while holding exitLock, then resumes them after unlocking. signalEOF follows the same broad pattern. The line reader likewise unlocks bufferLock before calling onLine, then locks again. These lines show useful callback boundaries. They do not prove that every helper path is race-free or that a runtime fault occurred.

The companion runs two thousand concurrent increments through NSLock, Mutex and the allocated unfair-lock wrapper, checking the exact final values. It also throws inside the classic wrapper and subsequently reads the value, testing cleanup on the error path. These are semantic checks, not fairness, throughput or contention measurements. A successful run cannot prove all schedules or correctness of every future wrapper mutation. Thread Sanitizer in an appropriate scratch target can provide additional race evidence, but no sanitizer result is claimed here.

Java synchronized monitors and ReentrantLock are familiar blocking counterparts, yet monitors are reentrant and ReentrantLock can be configured for fairness. NSLock, Mutex and unfair locks here are not recursive. kotlinx.coroutines Mutex suspends waiters and has different ownership semantics, so code that holds it across a suspension is not a template for NSLock. Use actors when isolation and asynchronous waiting fit the ownership model; use a short scoped synchronous lock when immediate callback state needs atomicity. The decision should include caller context, availability, contention risk, and evidence rather than a blanket claim that actors replace every lock.

quiz.question: Why is individually locking a counter getter and setter insufficient for increment?
options: Swift Int cannot be stored under a lock.
The read-modify-write transition can interleave between separately protected calls.
A Sendable constraint makes the increment atomic.
quiz.explanation: The invariant is the complete transition. Two readers can observe the same old value unless read and update share one critical section.

quiz.question: Which usage respects NSLock's thread ownership?
options: lock; await network(); unlock.
Acquire and release within one short synchronous scope, then await outside.
Unlock from any callback thread after cancellation.
quiz.explanation: Lock and unlock must match on the same thread. Await may suspend and resume elsewhere, and cancellation does not perform the unlock for you.

quiz.question: Why choose OSAllocatedUnfairLock over a raw os_unfair_lock Swift property?
options: It promises FIFO fairness.
It provides stable allocated lock storage and scoped state access.
It makes expensive locked work asynchronous.
quiz.explanation: Stable storage addresses the C lock's address requirement. It remains blocking, nonrecursive and without FIFO or deadline guarantees.

exercise.brief: Build a synchronous result box in your scratch copy. Two callbacks may try to finish it, but only the first may publish a result.
steps: Run the companion and read each of its three lock checks.
Define pending and finished states and install one completion callback.
Write finish so the first terminal call stores its result and takes the callback in one locked change.
Return the callback and result from the lock scope, then invoke it after unlocking.
Test success-first and error-first orders, plus a callback that immediately reads the box.
acceptance: Two competing finish calls produce exactly one completion.
Success-first and error-first runs each keep the first terminal result.
The completion runs after unlock and can read the box safely.
No thread-owned lock spans await. The chosen lock has a stated platform fallback.
exercise.solution:
Keep an optional terminal Result and an optional completion in one private state. finish(result) visits that state through update. If a result is already present, return nil. Otherwise store the result, remove the completion from the box, and return that callback with its result. Invoke it only after update returns and releases the lock. Checking the old state, setting the new state, and taking the callback must be one protected change. Separately locked helpers would let two callers both decide they won.

Install the completion before producers can run. Alternatively, define registration so it returns an already stored result and invokes the callback outside the lock. That alternative needs one atomic check-and-transfer too: registration can race with finish. A callback that immediately queries the box checks a useful failure case. After unlock it sees finished and can acquire the free lock. Calling it while holding NSLock would deadlock. An error is another terminal Result; it must not leave the box pending.

Use the small NSLock wrapper on older targets, Mutex where supported, or OSAllocatedUnfairLock with its stated platform floor. Keep callback storage private and never retain inout access beyond its closure. To turn this box into a cancellation-aware async bridge, also define how the stop token is registered and which path owns the continuation. A continuation is the means to resume the waiting task; it must have exactly one terminal outcome. Record deterministic orders and any stress run you actually perform. Neither proves every possible schedule. The shipped checks cover instructor code; the learner's result box remains separate work.

simple.story: A shared notebook says there is one apple in the cupboard. Priya and Sam each plan to add one. If both read one before either writes, both can write two, and one addition is lost. Put a key beside the notebook. Priya takes the key, reads one, writes two, and returns it. Sam then takes it, reads two, writes three, and returns it. The key must cover reading and writing together. After returning it, Priya can call someone to report the new count without stopping Sam from using the notebook.
simple.meaning: A lock protects a short synchronous change to shared state. All access paths must follow the same rule. Protect the whole read-modify-write, release the lock even on errors, and invoke callbacks afterward. Waiting for this kind of lock blocks a thread.

example.before: A protected result box is pending and owns one completion callback. No result is stored.
example.change: finish(.success(17)) wins the lock, stores the result, and removes the callback. A later finish(.failure(.fixture)) finds it finished.
example.after: The stored result stays .success(17). Only the first caller gets the callback, and it invokes it after unlocking, so completion happens once.

picture.caption: One locked state change chooses the result and hands the callback to its single caller.

items.label: Pending
items.text: There is no result and one callback belongs to the box.

items.label: Locked change
items.text: The first finish stores success(17) and removes the callback together.

items.label: Unlock and call
items.text: The winner invokes that callback after releasing the lock.

items.label: Later finish
items.text: The failure call sees finished and gets no callback to invoke.

words.meaning: A rule that every allowed state change must preserve, such as publishing a result only once.
The small part of code that accesses shared state while holding its lock.
A change other protected callers cannot observe halfway through.
A lock you cannot acquire again while you already hold it.
Rules that control access to an actor's state; an actor does not own a dedicated thread.
An author's promise of safe cross-domain use that the compiler does not prove.

simple.remember: Read, decide and write under one lock; notify after unlocking.
simple.boundary: A real lock does not make every reachable object safe. Every access must use the agreed boundary. NSLock blocks contending threads; Kotlin's coroutine Mutex can suspend waiting coroutines. An actor provides isolation and can allow interleaving at await.

lessons.title: Tasks and workers: CPU work, suspension and blocking reads
lessons.summary: Tell suspension from work that occupies a thread, limit admitted jobs, and give blocking reads an honest cancellation policy.
objectives: Identify code that occupies a worker thread and draw waits that could prevent progress.
Explain a CPU helper's execution boundary and its cooperative cancellation checks.
Limit how many child tasks are admitted and restore results to input order.
Wrap a blocking legacy read without promising instant cancellation or guaranteed priority.

sections.title: Waiting can free a thread or occupy it
sections.html:
If you leave a numbered ticket while waiting, the desk can help someone else. A task's suspension is similar: it keeps the information needed to continue and releases its current thread for other work. A synchronous wait instead occupies that thread until it returns. So do a synchronous file read and a long CPU loop. Swift tasks share execution resources; each task does not get a private thread. Android's Dispatchers.Default and Dispatchers.IO teach a useful CPU-versus-blocking distinction, but Swift has no universal one-line translation of those dispatcher choices. Also, reaching await does not guarantee suspension if the result is already available.

The cooperative runtime depends on forward progress. If all available workers block while waiting for tasks that need those workers, the dependency can starve or deadlock. Raising priority cannot create the missing progress guarantee. Even without a hard cycle, many large CPU jobs can delay visible results and cancellation handling. State the resource demand and wait graph before changing Task syntax.

Session 015 explains structured task lifetime, session 040 bounds network batches, and session 038 warns against main-actor CPU work. This lesson adds a concrete scheduling decision: how many jobs are admitted, where blocking work executes, and how cancellation frees ownership. An actor serializes isolated segments but is not a dedicated background thread. A Task created on MainActor can inherit that isolation. Detached work does not inherit the same actor or task-local context, and still uses cooperative execution rather than an unlimited blocking pool.

sections.title: Make the CPU boundary and stop checks explicit
sections.html:
A checksum adds input values. That loop uses CPU time even when its function is called async. The @concurrent annotation on the helper below makes its async execution leave the caller's actor. It does not assign a dedicated thread or split the loop into parallel pieces. A cancellation check asks whether stopping was requested, then throws if so. The companion requires Swift 6.2 tools and macOS 15. @concurrent is a compiler feature; that differs from a framework's OS availability. Earlier author verification recorded Swift 6.4, with no run claimed on the oldest supported compiler or OS.

@concurrent
func checksum(_ input: [Int]) async throws -> Int {
    var total = 0
    for (index, value) in input.enumerated() {
        if index.isMultiple(of: 256) { try Task.checkCancellation() }
        total += value
    }
    try Task.checkCancellation()
    return total
}

The underscore removes the external input label. [Int] is an array value that can cross this boundary safely; the loop's total is local to the task. enumerated supplies an offset and element, not a dictionary key. Checking at index zero observes already requested cancellation; checking every 256 values limits additional work between checks for this synthetic algorithm. The final check prevents returning an accepted result after the final loop segment if cancellation has become visible. throws propagates CancellationError. Small fixtures avoid Int overflow; a general numeric API needs a checked arithmetic policy.

Marking a function async does not split its loop into concurrent pieces. Cancellation checks inspect state without necessarily suspending. Task.yield can voluntarily offer a scheduling opportunity, but it does not guarantee another task runs, reserve fairness, or move actor-isolated work elsewhere. Choose chunk boundaries from correctness and measured response needs. Do not claim this fixture established a cancellation-latency budget; it establishes values and a pre-cancelled outcome.

sections.title: Limit waiting jobs as well as active jobs
sections.html:
A cupboard holding a thousand waiting parcels still needs room even if you unpack only two at once. Likewise, thousands of tasks waiting for permits retain their payloads and information needed to resume. Limiting active work alone does not limit this backlog. OperationQueue.maxConcurrentOperationCount also limits executing operations rather than the number added. An admission policy decides when to accept more work. State separate limits for active jobs, queued items and bytes, plus how to handle duplicates and urgent requests. Rejecting a request, replacing an obsolete one and suspending its producer are different product behaviours.

The host windowedChecksums creates at most width children initially and admits one replacement after group.next returns a completion. Each child returns an input index and value; only the parent writes the output array. Task-group completion order can differ from input order, so indexing restores the presentation contract without shared child mutation. A width of two is a synthetic policy, not a measured optimum or CPU-count formula. An empty input returns an empty array; a nonpositive width is an unsupported programmer input rejected by precondition.

The helper still receives an array holding every input batch, so it limits child admission rather than all retained memory. A stream or large archive also needs a bounded producer and a byte budget. Backpressure means preventing a producer from freely adding work when capacity is unavailable. Check cancellation before admitting the initial children and every replacement. Preserve thrown errors: a failing task-group scope cancels and joins unfinished children before leaving. A synchronous child that ignores cancellation can delay that join. Successful completion, a current request identity and bounded resource use are three separate requirements.

sections.title: Suspend the caller while another thread does the read
sections.html:
A blocking file read occupies the thread doing it until the read returns. Data(contentsOf:) is such a synchronous API. The companion places it in an OperationQueue with an execution limit of two and resumes a checked continuation when it finishes. A continuation records how to resume a suspended task. The async caller can therefore wait without occupying its current thread, while the operation still occupies its own thread during the read. This fixture performs only one read at a time. The queue's limit is extra protection, not a bound on backlog from an unlimited producer.

func read(_ url: URL) async throws -> Data {
    try Task.checkCancellation()
    let data: Data = try await withCheckedThrowingContinuation { continuation in
        queue.addOperation {
            do { continuation.resume(returning: try Data(contentsOf: url)) }
            catch { continuation.resume(throwing: error) }
        }
    }
    try Task.checkCancellation()
    return data
}

This method belongs to the companion's BlockingFileReader class, whose private queue is configured during initialization. The initial check avoids an already cancelled read. withCheckedThrowingContinuation parks the task; the operation has exactly one success or error resumption. Data is returned as a value. The final check discards a completed read if cancellation was requested meanwhile. There is deliberately no cancellation handler claiming to interrupt Data(contentsOf:): cancellation can wait until an in-flight read returns. A thrown file error propagates rather than becoming empty data.

A more capable legacy API may expose a cancellable handle. Bridging it requires synchronized registration, cancellation-before-registration behavior and exactly-once terminal resumption. Cancelling a queued BlockOperation without resuming its continuation would strand the caller. Conversely, resuming early while releasing resources still used by a running read can violate ownership. Define cancellation latency and cleanup honestly. Prefer an already asynchronous API for network transport; this isolated adapter demonstrates a boundary for unavoidable legacy blocking work.

sections.title: An urgency hint does not reserve capacity
sections.html:
An urgent label can influence which work runs, but it cannot manufacture a free disk, lock or worker. Task priority and dispatch quality of service communicate importance to the scheduler. They do not promise deadlines, first-in-first-out order, or interruption of a synchronous callback already running. Waiting relationships may raise a task's effective priority, but correctness must not depend on one urgent task always overtaking every less urgent task. Actors also do not promise complete async requests run in submission order: a suspended request can allow another isolated segment to run.

Priority inversion occurs when visible work waits for a resource held by less urgent work. Avoid long critical sections, reserve capacity for visible demand, replace obsolete speculative jobs, and stop admitting prefetches when foreground needs the resource. Separate queues alone do not make a shared disk, lock or memory bandwidth independent. A burst of userInitiated tasks can still consume the resource needed by the UI. Escalating all work erases useful distinctions and may increase energy cost.

Use application-level ordering where the requirement is a deadline or fairness policy. An admission owner can select visible jobs before prefetches, age waiting jobs to prevent starvation, and record an explicit maximum backlog. Do not claim OS scheduling implemented that policy because a priority enum was passed. Kotlin withContext also switches execution context without inventing request-rate limits or a fair product queue. Java fixed pools bound worker count but can retain unbounded queues unless configured otherwise. The boundary is resource ownership, not the similarity of APIs named task or executor.

sections.title: Ask what detached work owns and retains
sections.html:
A detached task starts work without inheriting the caller's actor or task-local values. It still uses Swift's cooperative execution resources. The inspected timeslots provider creates Task.detached(priority: .userInitiated), first reduces remaining IDs synchronously, then awaits combined.async and either fulfils or rejects a PromiseKit result. These lines show a chosen priority and CPU work before a possible suspension. They do not show that the reduction is expensive, that cancellation propagates, or that the feature starves other work. Answer those questions with caller ownership, effective annotations, representative input sizes and execution evidence.

A defensible review asks who owns the detached handle, how a superseded query stops admission, how many IDs and retained values occur, and which error becomes visible. Then instrument the operation boundary in a separate approved performance investigation. Compare foreground response distributions, cancellation latency, queue depth and bytes retained under identical fixtures and device conditions. The host checks here do not provide those measurements. Moving reduction to an actor would change serialization without necessarily adding cancellation or backlog control.

The companion checks small indexed checksum values, a gated cancellation requested before CPU execution, and one file-read success plus one real missing-file error. The gate is always released; it never deliberately exhausts executor workers or runs a deadlock demonstration. These tests establish useful semantics while leaving in-flight I/O cancellation, overload policy under load, physical-device starvation traces and energy tradeoffs as explicit further investigations. A learner should carry forward an admission and lifetime design, with the verified boundary stated, rather than treat a passing CLI as production scheduler certification.

quiz.question: Does Task.detached create an unlimited blocking-I/O thread pool?
options: Yes, one dedicated thread per detached task.
No; it is unstructured work using cooperative execution, with separate ownership obligations.
Only when priority is background.
quiz.explanation: Detached changes inherited context and structure, not the forward-progress requirement. Blocking work still needs a bounded adapter or async API.

quiz.question: What does the windowed task-group helper bound?
options: All input memory and requests per second.
The initially created/in-flight child window; the input array is still retained.
A hard cancellation latency deadline.
quiz.explanation: Admission bounds child count. Byte budgets, streaming input, request rate and latency require independent policies and evidence.

quiz.question: Why does BlockingFileReader check cancellation after its continuation returns?
options: It forcibly interrupts the completed read.
It prevents returning accepted data after cancellation while honestly waiting for an in-flight legacy call.
It changes an Operation into a structured child task.
quiz.explanation: The legacy synchronous call is not interrupted. Post-read checking enforces the chosen result policy; operation cancellation and lifetime remain separately wired.

exercise.brief: Add a small indexed checksum case in your scratch copy. Then plan limits and cancellation for visible file reads competing with prefetch.
steps: Predict the sums for [[7], [], [2, 3], [4]] at width 2 before adding the case in your scratch copy.
Return an input index from every child. Let only the parent write the output array.
Choose separate limits for active jobs, waiting jobs and retained bytes.
Describe what happens if cancellation is requested before enqueueing and after a noninterruptible read starts.
Plan how to compare visible reads with prefetch under representative load, naming the evidence you would record.
acceptance: The ordered sums are [7, 0, 5, 4], and children do not mutate shared output.
Width is validated, and observed cancellation stops the parent from admitting replacements.
Limits cover waiting payloads as well as executing operations.
No cooperative task blocks on a semaphore, and no thread-owned lock stays held across await.
The report separates executed host checks from load tests and device measurements still to be done.
exercise.solution:
Keep the output array in the parent and make each child return its input index with its sum. Start two children. Await a completion, store the sum at that child's index, then start one replacement. This yields [7, 0, 5, 4] even if completion order differs. Before the first admissions and every replacement, check for a cancellation request. Once the parent observes one, stop adding work. If a child throws, preserve its error; the structured task-group scope cancels and joins remaining children instead of returning a successful-looking partial array.

For visible reads competing with prefetch, give one owner the admission decisions. Set an active limit of two, a named pending-item limit and a synthetic byte budget. Reserve an opportunity for visible work, or give it the next released slot. Replace older prefetches for the same identity rather than accumulating them. These numbers are design inputs to test, not device measurements or recommended optimums. Keep tokens for pending requests so a stop request can remove a waiting item and resume its caller with CancellationError exactly once.

Once a noninterruptible read starts, keep its resources valid until it returns. Record the cancellation request and reject or discard the eventual result according to your policy. Do not close a descriptor still in use. The supplied bridge instead waits for completion and checks cancellation afterward, a simpler policy for this fixture. Record backlog, retained bytes and foreground latency only in a workload experiment that actually measures them. Higher QoS and Task.detached do not define those limits. The earlier instructor checks support the mechanics; they do not complete your added fixture or establish a production rollout.

simple.story: A repair desk accepts four phones. It allows two repairs to be active at once. When a repair needs an outside part, the clerk records where to continue and serves another customer while waiting. That is different from holding the counter closed until the part arrives. Polishing a phone also keeps someone busy even though it involves no waiting. The desk starts the next repair only when one active repair ends. Each phone keeps its numbered ticket, so the finished phones can be returned in ticket order even when repairs finish in a different order.
simple.meaning: Suspension lets a task wait without occupying its current thread. Synchronous CPU work and blocking I/O occupy a thread until they return. A bounded task window limits child admission, and indexed results preserve input order. @concurrent leaves caller-actor execution; it does not create a private thread.

example.before: The inputs are [[7], [], [2, 3], [4]], with width 2. Children for indices 0 and 1 start first.
example.change: Process each completed child by storing its value at its input index, then admit one replacement while inputs remain.
example.after: Once all children finish, output is [7, 0, 5, 4], regardless of completion order. At most two children are outstanding; the input array still retains all four batches.

words.meaning: The runtime mechanism that arranges where ready task work executes.
Pausing a task at a possible await point without keeping its current thread occupied.
Keeping a thread occupied until a synchronous operation or wait returns.
Deciding when to start more work and how much may be outstanding.
The ability of work needed by other work to get a chance to execute.

simple.boundary: Tasks are not repair clerks or private threads. An await may complete without suspending. Actor isolation controls access, while workers execute ready segments. Width 2 is a synthetic policy, not a measured best value or a bound on all input memory.
